extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, and readers of English legal doctrine (Blackstone's Commentaries)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of English common-law rules and statutory provisions governing validity and dissolution of marriage, legal effects of marriage (coverture), and parental duties and powers toward legitimate children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a valid civil marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The law treats marriage as a civil contract and requires that parties (1) be willing to contract, (2) be able to contract, and (3) actually do contract in the proper forms and solemnities required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'holiness' of matrimony is for ecclesiastical law; temporal courts consider only civil validity. The threefold test (willing, able, did contract) governs whether a matrimonial contract is good and valid for civil purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent as essential element
rubrics_metrics.description: "Consensus, non concubitus, facit nuptias" — consent, not sexual intercourse, makes a marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willing consent is a fundamental requirement adopted from civil and canon law; lack of consent (e.g., forcible marriage) affects civil and criminal consequences and evidentiary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical impediments (voidable marriages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical disabilities (e.g., pre-contract, consanguinity, affinity, some corporal infirmities) are sufficient by ecclesiastical law to avoid the marriage, but in common law make the marriage voidable, not ipso facto void, until sentence of nullity is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These impediments are primarily for ecclesiastical courts (pro salute animarum). Such marriages are treated as valid for civil purposes unless annulled during the parties' lives; after death common law courts will not permit the spiritual courts to declare them void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limitation of impediments to Levitical degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute 32 Hen. VIII c. 38 declares that nothing shall impeach any marriage except those prohibited by God's law and within the Levitical degrees, the farthest being uncle and niece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute also declares marriages celebrated in the face of the church and consummated to be indissoluble. Historical statutory changes (e.g., repeal of parts by 2 & 3 Edw. VI c.23) and later statutes (e.g., 26 Geo. II c.33) affect related doctrines such as pre-contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil disabilities that render marriage void ab initio
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain municipal-law-created disabilities render persons incapable of forming any matrimonial contract at all; such marriages are void ab initio (not merely voidable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These civil disabilities are regarded as preventing the junction rather than dissolving an existing union; unions entered into by persons under these disabilities are meretricious, not matrimonial, in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior marriage (bigamy) — incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior subsisting marriage (having another husband or wife living) is a legal disability which makes a second marriage void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bigamy is condemned and the second marriage is void; it also carries penalties (felony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of consent for marriage (common-law ages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under common law, a boy under fourteen or a girl under twelve who marries have only an inchoate and imperfect marriage; upon reaching the age of consent they may disaffirm the marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canon law may treat capacity differently (habiles ad matrimonium). If at age of consent the parties agree to continue together, a new marriage need not be solemnized. Mutuality of consent required when only one spouse reaches age of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental/guardian consent and licence/banns formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: By common law, if parties were of age of consent no parental concurrence was needed, but statutes penalize clergy marrying without publication of banns or licence (which involves parental consent for minors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes (e.g., 4 & 5 Phil. & Mary c.8; 26 Geo. II c.33) impose penalties and may render marriages by licence where either party is under 21 without parental/guardian consent absolutely void; banns give notice to parents. Lord Chancellor may dispense in cases where guardian is non compos or absent; widow/widower exceptions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental capacity (want of reason) as incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Want of reason (idiots and lunatics) is an incapacity to contract marriage; judges and statutes treat deprivations of reason as impediments to valid marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old common law allowed such persons to marry; statute 15 Geo. II c.30 and judicial development remedy defects with regard to lunatics and persons under frenzies; idiots are regarded within the reason of that statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality requirements for celebration of marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: A marriage must be celebrated in a parish church or public chapel (unless special dispensation) and preceded by publication of banns or by licence; performed by a person in orders is held essential by positive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal contracts per verba de praesenti or, with cohabitation, per verba de futuro were previously effective for many purposes but the statute (26 Geo. II c.33) curtailed verbal contracts to compel future marriage. Neglect of some formalities may be penal but not necessarily invalidate the marriage; special dispensations can permit marriages elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of consummation on indissolubility
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriages contracted in the face of the church and consummated with bodily knowledge and fruit of children are declared indissoluble by statute (32 Hen. VIII c.38).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consummation is an important factor in statutory protection of marriage from dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Void vs. voidable timing and effect (canonical v. civil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical impediments make a marriage voidable (requiring ecclesiastical sentence to annul); civil disabilities make it void ab initio; ecclesiastical annulments cannot be declared after death of a party for civil purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total divorces a vinculo matrimonii must be for canonical causes existing before marriage; ecclesiastical courts act pro salute animarum and their decrees have temporal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of divorce and their grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of divorce: (1) total (a vinculo matrimonii) — declares marriage null as unlawful ab initio, usually for canonical causes existing before marriage; (2) partial (a mensa et thoro) — separation from bed and board for supervenient causes (intolerable ill temper, adultery, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canon law disfavours dissolution for causes arising after union; civil law allowed more causes historically. In England adultery traditionally gives rise to separation (mensa et thoro) rather than total divorce, though acts of Parliament have sometimes granted total divorce for adultery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alimony on separation (a mensa et thoro)
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of divorce a mensa et thoro, the law allows alimony to the wife, an allowance for support out of the husband's estate, settled at the discretion of the ecclesiastical judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alimony (estovers) is proportioned to rank and quality of the parties; if husband refuses payment remedies include excommunication and writ de estoveriis habendis. No alimony allowed where wife elopes and lives with an adulterer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal unity of spouses (coverture) and its doctrinal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: By marriage the husband and wife are one person in law: the woman's legal existence is suspended or incorporated into that of the husband (feme-covert), and her condition during marriage is called coverture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include inability of husband to grant to wife or enter covenant with her; compacts made between husband and wife when single are generally voided by intermarriage; wife may act as attorney for husband; husband may bequeath to wife by will; husband bound to provide necessaries and pay debts for necessaries; if wife elopes husband not chargeable for necessaries when supplier is apprized; wife injured cannot sue without husband's concurrence (civil), though criminal prosecutions proceed separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony and evidentiary rules between spouses
rubrics_metrics.description: Husband and wife are not allowed to be evidence for or against each other in trials, except in cases where the offence is directly against the person of the wife or where the marriage lacked consent (e.g., forcible marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles cited: nemo in propria causa testis esse debet and nemo tenetur seipsum accusare. Statute 3 Hen. VII c.2 permits a woman carried away and married to be a witness against such husband in felony cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical law distinction: spouses as separate persons
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil (Roman) law and in ecclesiastical courts the husband and wife are considered two distinct persons, able to have separate estates, contracts, debts, and injuries; hence a woman may sue and be sued without her husband in ecclesiastical courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with common-law coverture and affects remedies available in different jurisdictions (temporal vs spiritual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of deeds and acts by married woman during coverture
rubrics_metrics.description: Deeds executed and acts done by a woman during her coverture are void or voidable, except fines or matters of record where a secret examination is required to learn if her act was voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law assumes coercion during coverture; special procedural protections (examination) apply to validate some acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on wife's testamentary disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A married woman cannot by will devise lands to her husband except under special circumstances because she is supposed to be under his coercion when making it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverture affects testamentary capacity and the admissibility of dispositions in favour of husband.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal and civil liability differences for married women
rubrics_metrics.description: In criminal prosecutions a wife may be indicted and punished separately; in civil matters she often cannot sue or be sued without her husband's concurrence and name, with certain statutory exceptions (e.g., abjuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union is primarily a civil one; statutory and judicial exceptions exist to avoid injustice (e.g., where husband is abjured or in forcible marriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband's historical power of correction and modern limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the husband might give his wife moderate correction; this power was confined within reasonable bounds, but later practice allowed wives to obtain security of the peace against husbands and courts to restrain excessive correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the old rule persists in some popular practice among lower ranks, courts will permit restraint or security where misbehaviour is gross; power of correction does not extend to treason or murder and is limited by law and public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental duties to legitimate children: maintenance, protection, education
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents owe three principal duties to legitimate children: maintenance, protection, and education; maintenance is a principle of natural law and municipal laws enforce the obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats these duties as natural obligations reinforced by law; maintenance is a child's right; education is emphasised as of greatest importance though municipal law rarely enforces it for the rich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and practical rules for maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes make the father, mother, grandfather, and grandmother of poor impotent persons liable to maintain them in proportion to ability as directed by quarter sessions; churchwardens may seize a parent's property to relieve abandoned children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mother or grandmother marries again, the husband may be charged to maintain the child; there are limits — no one is bound to maintain children unless they are impotent/unable to work; penalty for refusal often set (e.g., 20s per month).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and special provisions regarding religious coercion and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes (e.g., 11 & 12 W. III c.4; 1 Ann. st.1 c.30) address parents who coerce children religiously — for example, penalising popish or jewish parents who refuse to maintain protestant children or who send children abroad to popish institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties include fines, forfeiture of goods/real estate for life, and disabilities (unable to sue or hold office). The lord chancellor may enforce maintenance in some cases involving religious coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customary and testamentary protections for children and heirs
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom of London entitled children of freemen to one third of father's effects (inalienable by will); courts favour heirs and children, requiring utmost certainty of words to disinherit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although law generally allows testamentary freedom, certain customs and principles protect children's expected shares; courts will set aside wills for defective motives or insufficient clarity when disinheriting heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power derived from duty, variable by jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental power is derived from duty to children and varies by law: Roman patria potestas was extensive (even life/death); English law is more moderate but still allows authority to keep child in order, defend them, and manage their affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include justifying an assault in defence of a child and other allowances reflecting parental authority tempered by modern sensibilities and statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticing poor children as statutory education/relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes provide apprenticeship for poor and laborious children past age of nurture, removing them from parental hands to breed useful skills for the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one instance where law intervenes to secure education/training of children; for the rich education remains largely at parental discretion.
